doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Translating the blues to the drum kit
summary: Drummers think in rhythms rather than changes, drawing on life and on childhood memories of a grandmother's lullaby.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Now I want to ask you a question. I know that you’re capable of this because you just talked about it. But when you think of the blues, you think of either a blues singer, a blues guitar player ‘cause he can bend them strings, or maybe a sax player, but how do you transfer those sounds to the drum kit?

Well rhythm is our business. See we don’t play changes on drums. We play rhythms. So we think in terms of, you see somebody walking down the street, it takes a certain rhythm. You think about life, you know what I’m saying? And you take your music and you express what you live and what you see, you see what I mean? The blues is something, it’s a feeling that should be in you. From your grandmother, sitting on your grandmother’s lap and she say, you know, “go to sleep little baby.” You know what I’m saying? [sings] “Baby.” So that’s in you from a kid you know. So you know you go to school to learn academics, so that you can play with a bunch of guys that you don’t even know, because you have the music. But you should never forget what’s in your heart, what you learned from your grandma, you know?
